chapters.title: Chapter 3: Understanding Your Income and Tax

lessons.title: Common Deductions and Exemptions: 80C, 80D, HRA and More

body.text: A deduction is worth your tax rate, not its face value. ₹1,50,000 under 80C saves ₹46,800 in the 30% slab, ₹7,800 in the 5% slab, and nothing at all if the new regime already gives you a lower tax.

children.text: The last lesson helped you pick a regime. If you chose the old one, this lesson is about claiming every deduction you are entitled to, and nothing you are not. If you chose the new one, read the NPS section closely: it is the one major deduction that survives. Remember that Chapter 2 already covered the documents; here we focus on the rules.
Exemptions vs Deductions: Know Which Is Which

body.title: Two Ways to Reduce Taxable Income

Mostly salary allowances: HRA and LTA
Sit in Schedule III of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 10 of the 1961 Act)

Investments and spends: 80C, 80D, NPS, donations, education loan interest
Sit in Sections 122 to 154 of the 2025 Act (Chapter VI-A of the 1961 Act)
Selected one by one from a dropdown in the ITR
Almost all old regime only, except the employer's NPS contribution

body.title: Tax Saved by a Full ₹1,50,000 Under 80C, Including Cess

children.text: Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80C of the Income-tax Act, 1961) allows up to ₹1,50,000 a year for a list of investments and payments. Contributions to pension plans and your own NPS contribution under 80CCD(1) share the same ₹1,50,000 ceiling. The mistake most salaried people make is not under-investing; it is buying products they don't need to fill a limit their EPF has already half filled.

body.title: Which One Does Not Count?
body.question: Anjali, an engineer at L&T in Chennai, is filling her 80C claims. Which of these payments does NOT qualify?
options: Tuition fees paid to her son's CBSE school
The principal portion of her home loan EMIs from SBI
Fees for her daughter's JEE coaching classes
Premium on a term insurance policy for her husband
body.explanation: Only tuition fees for full-time education at a school, college or university qualify. Private coaching fees do not, nor do development fees or donations to the school. Home loan principal and life insurance premiums for a spouse both qualify.

body.title: Over the Limit Without Realising
body.prompt: Arvind, a manager in Kolkata, has a basic salary of ₹60,000 a month and contributes 12% of it to EPF. He also put ₹30,000 in PPF, paid ₹24,000 in LIC premiums, and paid ₹45,000 in school tuition fees for his two children. By how much does his total 80C spending exceed the amount he can actually deduct?
body.explanation: EPF is 12% of ₹60,000 = ₹7,200 a month, or ₹86,400 a year. Total 80C spend: ₹86,400 + ₹30,000 + ₹24,000 + ₹45,000 = ₹1,85,400. The deduction is capped at ₹1,50,000, so ₹35,400 gives no tax benefit. If he bought the LIC policy only to save tax, his EPF and tuition fees alone already came close to filling the limit.

children.text: NPS: Three Deductions in One Account

body.caption: NPS Deductions Under Section 124 of the 2025 Act (Section 80CCD of the 1961 Act)

cells: Up to 10% of salary, within the ₹1,50,000 ceiling shared with 80C
Up to 14% of salary in the new regime; 10% in the old regime for private sector employees

body.text: The employer NPS contribution is the most valuable deduction left in the new regime. Salary here means basic plus DA. With a basic of ₹10,00,000, up to ₹1,40,000 of employer contribution is deductible, saving ₹43,680 for someone in the 30% slab. If your employer offers it, restructuring part of your CTC into employer NPS can cut tax without changing your regime. One cap to watch: employer contributions to NPS, EPF and superannuation above ₹7,50,000 a year in total become a taxable perquisite.

children.text: Section 80D: Health Insurance for Your Family and Parents

Section 126 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80D of the 1961 Act) has two separate buckets: one for yourself, your spouse and dependent children, and one for your parents. Each has its own limit, which doubles if the people covered in that bucket include a senior citizen.

cells: Up to ₹5,000, within the limits above
Up to ₹5,000, within the limits above
Medical bills of an uninsured senior citizen
Within the ₹50,000 limit for that bucket

body.title: Work Out Nisha's 80D
body.prompt: Nisha, 42, lives in Ahmedabad. In FY 2025-26 she paid, by net banking, ₹28,000 for a family floater covering herself, her husband and two children, and ₹46,000 for a health policy covering her father, 71, and mother, 66. She also paid ₹8,000 by UPI for preventive health check-ups for her own family. What is her total 80D deduction?
body.explanation: Family bucket: the limit is ₹25,000 as everyone is below 60. Her ₹28,000 premium already exceeds it, so the check-ups add nothing, since they sit within the same limit rather than on top. Family deduction: ₹25,000. Parents bucket: both parents are senior citizens, so the limit is ₹50,000, and her ₹46,000 premium is fully deductible. Total: ₹25,000 + ₹46,000 = ₹71,000.

body.text: Three 80D traps. First, premiums paid in cash are not deductible; only preventive check-ups can be paid in cash. Second, premiums for siblings, in-laws or grandparents do not qualify. Third, if you pay a multi-year premium upfront, the deduction is spread evenly over the years the policy covers, not claimed in full in the year of payment.

children.text: A home loan EMI has two parts, and each is claimed differently. The principal goes into the 80C basket. The interest is claimed under the house property head, under Section 22 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 24(b) of the 1961 Act).

body.title: 80GG for a Freelancer
body.prompt: Tanvi, a freelance content writer in Jaipur, receives no HRA because she is not an employee. She has opted for the old regime, pays rent of ₹15,000 a month, and her adjusted total income for FY 2025-26 is ₹6,00,000. She owns no house anywhere. What is her deduction for rent paid?
body.explanation: The three limbs: ₹5,000 × 12 = ₹60,000; 25% of ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,50,000; rent of ₹1,80,000 minus 10% of ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,20,000. The lowest is ₹60,000. That ₹5,000 a month cap is why 80GG is far less generous than HRA for anyone paying meaningful rent.

body.title: Audit Vikas's Deduction Claims
body.scenario: Vikas, 45, a sales head in Lucknow, is in the old regime. His draft ITR claims: 80C of ₹1,50,000, which includes ₹40,000 of JEE coaching fees for his son; 80D of ₹60,000 for his parents, aged 58 and 55, of which ₹20,000 was paid in cash; 80G of ₹10,000 for a cash donation to a registered temple trust; 80CCD(1B) of ₹50,000, paid to his NPS account through net banking; and 80TTA of ₹14,000, equal to his savings account interest. Total claimed: ₹2,84,000.
body.prompt: Correct each claim. What is the total deduction Vikas can actually take, and how much of his original claim would be disallowed?
body.modelAnswer: 80C: coaching fees do not qualify, so remove ₹40,000, leaving ₹1,10,000. 80D: his parents are both below 60, so the limit is ₹25,000; the ₹20,000 paid in cash does not count, leaving ₹40,000 of eligible premium, which is capped at ₹25,000. 80G: cash donations above ₹2,000 are not deductible, so the ₹10,000 goes to nil. 80CCD(1B): the ₹50,000 NPS contribution by net banking is valid. 80TTA: the deduction is capped at ₹10,000 even though his interest was ₹14,000; the full ₹14,000 is still reported as income. Corrected total: ₹1,10,000 + ₹25,000 + ₹0 + ₹50,000 + ₹10,000 = ₹1,95,000. That is ₹89,000 less than he claimed. Filing the original version would have invited a mismatch notice or disallowance, with tax and interest on the difference. With ₹40,000 of room left in 80C, he could consider topping it up next year with a genuine investment rather than a coaching bill.

body.title: Deduction Check Before You File
steps: Confirm you are in the old regime; if not, only employer NPS, the standard deduction and a few others apply
Start 80C with what already counts: EPF from Form 16, tuition fees and home loan principal, before adding anything else
Check whether you are using the extra ₹50,000 for your own NPS under 80CCD(1B)
Split 80D into the family bucket and the parents bucket and apply the right limit to each
Remove anything paid in cash that the law disallows: health premiums and donations above ₹2,000
Get home loan interest and principal figures from your lender's certificate, not your own estimate
Match every claim to a document with the details the ITR dropdown asks for

points: Exemptions like HRA and LTA reduce salary income and now sit in Schedule III; deductions like 80C and 80D reduce gross total income and sit in Sections 122 to 154 of the 2025 Act
A deduction saves tax at your marginal rate, so ₹1,50,000 under 80C is worth ₹46,800 at 30% and only ₹7,800 at 5%
Section 123 (80C) caps at ₹1,50,000 including EPF, tuition fees and home loan principal, so check what already counts before buying products
Section 124 (80CCD) gives an extra ₹50,000 for your own NPS in the old regime, and the employer's contribution, up to 14% of salary, is deductible even in the new regime
Section 126 (80D) has separate family and parents buckets of ₹25,000 each, doubling to ₹50,000 where a senior citizen is covered, with no deduction for cash premiums
Home loan interest on a self-occupied house is capped at ₹2,00,000 under Section 22 (24(b)), and 80E, 80G, 80GG and 80TTA each have their own conditions worth checking

Deduction limits, conditions and section numbers reflect FY 2025-26 and the Income-tax Act, 2025 at the time of writing and can change.
